questions.question: Which muscle originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus?

explanation.text: The muscle that originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus is the pronator teres muscle. The pronator teres is located in the forearm and is responsible for pronating the forearm, which means rotating the forearm from a palm-up (supine) position to a palm-down (pronated) position.

Incorrect Options: Option A. Supinator: The supinator muscle, situated in the forearm's posterior compartment, isn't rooted in the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Option B. Pronator quadratus: The pronator quadratus muscle, deep in the forearm, isn't linked to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Option D. Brachioradialis: The brachioradialis muscle originates from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus, not the medial epicondyle.

questions.question: Identify the type of joint shown in the given image.

explanation.text: The image is of the middle radio ulnar joint which is formed by the interosseous ligament. This is a type of fibrous joint which is syndesmosis. The syndesmosis is a type of joint that is formed by the union of two bones by a strong, fibrous tissue called a ligament. This type of joint is found in areas where stability is more important than mobility, such as the distal tibiofibular joint in the ankle and the distal radioulnar joint in the wrist.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Symphysis: Symphysis joints fuse two bones with fibrocartilage, allowing limited movement crucial for shock absorption and flexibility, like in the pelvis and spine. Option C - Synchondrosis: Synchondrosis joints are formed by hyaline cartilage connecting two bones, commonly found in areas of growth and development like children's epiphyseal plates.
Option D - Synostosis: Synostosis occurs when bones fuse due to various reasons like trauma or congenital conditions, leading to no mobility. Examples include cranial suture and radius-ulna fusion.

questions.question: Which single muscle is involved in the actions of arm's flexion, adduction and medial rotation?

explanation.text: Pectoralis major muscle is involved in the actions of arm's flexion, adduction, and medial rotation. It is a large muscle located in the chest region and plays a significant role in various movements of the shoulder joint. Incorrect options: Option A. Serratus Anterior: This muscle is primarily involved in protraction and upward rotation of the scapula.

Option C. Pectoralis minor: This muscle assists in stabilizing the scapula and has a role in protraction and downward rotation of the scapula. Option D. Subclavius: This muscle helps to stabilize and depress the clavicle.

questions.question: The rotator cuff includes the following muscles all except;

explanation.text: The teres major muscle is not considered part of the rotator cuff. It is a larger muscle located on the posterior side of the upper arm and is responsible for adduction and medial rotation of the arm. Incorrect Options: Options A. Supraspinatus: The supraspinatus muscle is one of the four muscles that make up the rotator cuff. It is located on the posterior side of the shoulder joint and assists in shoulder abduction.

Options B. Infraspinatus: The infraspinatus muscle is another muscle that is part of the rotator cuff. It is situated below the supraspinatus muscle and is responsible for lateral rotation of the arm. Options D. Teres minor: The teres minor muscle is also included in the rotator cuff. It is located below the infraspinatus muscle and aids in lateral rotation of the arm.

questions.question: A 22-year-old male patient after an injury presented with a deformity as shown in the image. Which nerve will be damaged in the given condition?

explanation.text: In the given scenario, the image displaying wrist drop and a fracture of the shaft of the humerus is indicative of damage to the radial nerve Incorrect Options: Option A - Ulnar Nerve: The ulnar nerve mainly innervates forearm and hand muscles for wrist flexion and finger abduction. It's not typically involved in wrist drop.

Option C - Median Nerve: The median nerve innervates specific forearm muscles and the hand's anterior compartment but isn't heavily involved in wrist extension, the main problem in the image. Option D - Musculocutaneous Nerve: The musculocutaneous nerve mainly innervates the anterior arm muscles, like the biceps brachii, aiding in elbow flexion, not wrist extension.

questions.question: Which bone is most likely to be fractured in an injury to the anatomical snuff box?

explanation.text: The anatomical snuff box is a triangular depression located on the radial aspect of the dorsum (back) of the hand. It is formed by the tendons of the extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis muscles. Fractures within the anatomical snuff box are commonly associated with falls onto an outstretched hand, particularly with the wrist extended. The most fractured bone in this region is the scaphoid bone, also known as the navicular bone.

Incorrect Options: Option B - Lunar (lunate) bone: The lunate bone, found in the wrist joint, rarely fractures in injuries to the anatomical snuff box and isn't usually part of its formation. Option C - Cuboid bone: The cuboid bone is one of the tarsal bones located in the foot. It is not related to the anatomical snuff box or the wrist region. Option D - Trapezius: The trapezius is a large muscle located in the upper back and neck area.
It is not a bone and is not related to the anatomical snuff box or wrist injuries.

questions.question: The given finding is associated with ?

explanation.text: Trisomy 21, commonly known as Down syndrome, results from an extra copy of chromosome 21. People with Down syndrome often have distinct facial features, intellectual disabilities, and certain medical problems. Approximately half of individuals with Down syndrome have a single transverse palmar crease, making this the correct answer. The simian crease is relatively common in Down syndrome.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Trisomy 13: Trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome, results from an extra chromosome 13, leading to severe developmental issues and congenital abnormalities. While hand anomalies are common, a simian crease isn't typically present.

Option C - Klinefelter's syndrome: Klinefelter's syndrome in males with an extra X chromosome (XXY) leads to male hypogonadism and physical differences, but it's not usually linked to a simian crease. Option D - Trisomy 18: Trisomy 18, or Edwards syndrome, stems from an extra chromosome 18, leading to severe developmental delays, intellectual disabilities, and congenital anomalies.
While hand abnormalities may occur, a simian crease isn't a defining trait.

questions.question: The marked muscle is supplied by which nerve?

explanation.text: The muscle that is marked in the diagram is the biceps brachii. The three muscles innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve in the anterior part of the arm: biceps brachii, coracobrachialis, and brachialis. The terminal branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus is the musculocutaneous nerve. Incorrect Options: Option A - Radial nerve supplies the triceps brachii, brachioradialis, etc. it does not supply the biceps brachii.

Option B - Ulnar nerve does not supply biceps brachii. It innervates the forearm and hand muscles Option C - Median nerve does not supply biceps brachii. Some of the muscles innervated by the median nerve are flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, etc.

questions.question: Which of the subsequent structures of the brachial plexus does not provide any branches?

explanation.text: Division does not give branches in the Brachial Plexus. However, the Root, cords, trunks in the brachial plexus do give branches. Incorrect Options: Options A, B & C: Root, Cord and Tunks give branches

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about the lesion of the structure indicated by the arrow?

explanation.text: The lesion marked by the arrow leads to wrist drop. Wrist drop refers to a condition where the wrist is unable to maintain an extended position and hangs in a flexed position. It occurs due to weakness or paralysis of the muscles that extend the wrist, particularly the extensor muscles in the posterior compartment of the forearm. The most common cause of wrist drop is damage or compression of the radial nerve, which innervates these muscles.

Incorrect Options: Option A. Ape thumb deformity is when the thumb aligns more with the fingers, resembling an ape's thumb. It often occurs due to median nerve injuries.. Option B. Claw hand is a deformity marked by hyperextended metacarpophalangeal joints and flexed interphalangeal joints, giving the hand a claw-like look. It's commonly linked to ulnar nerve injuries.
Option C. Claudication is muscle pain due to poor blood flow during exercise, often in lower limbs, linked to peripheral artery disease.

questions.question: Identify the structure marked in the image given below:-

explanation.text: Option B-Ulnar Artery: The structure marked in the image is the ulnar artery. The ulnar artery is one of the main arteries in the forearm and hand. It runs along the ulnar side (medial side) of the forearm and supplies blood to the muscles and tissues of the forearm and hand.

Incorrect Options: Option A. The structure marked in the image isn't the ulnar nerve, which provides motor and sensory innervation to the hand and forearm as a separate anatomical entity. Option C. The structure in the image isn't the superficial radial artery, which is situated on the radial (lateral) side of the forearm, nearer to the skin surface.
Option D. The structure in the image isn't the median nerve, a major nerve in the arm that provides motor and sensory innervation to the hand and forearm.

questions.question: What is the function of the muscle indicated in the provided image?

explanation.text: The muscle marked in the question is the supraspinatus, which is present above the spine of the scapula and helps abduct the shoulder joint. The muscles involved in abducting the shoulder joint are the deltoid muscle, supraspinatus muscle, and the trapezius muscle Incorrect Options: Option A - Retraction of scapula: The muscles involved in retracting the scapula are the middle and lower trapezius muscles and the rhomboid major and minor muscles.

Option B - Protraction of scapula: The muscles involved in protracting the scapula are the serratus anterior muscle. Option D - Adduction of shoulder joint: The muscles involved in adducting the shoulder joint are the latissimus dorsi muscle, pectoralis major muscle, and the teres major muscle.

questions.question: Which among the following aids in supination and pronation of the forearm?

explanation.text: The forearm's radius and ulna bones are connected at the elbow joint to the upper arm's humerus bone. This joint allows for rotational movements like supination (palm up) and

pronation (palm down) as the radius rotates around the stationary ulna. It's a pivot joint, permitting movement around a single axis, supported by ligaments and muscles for stability and control of motion range. Incorrect Options: Option B - Saddle joint: A saddle joint in the thumb enables a wide range of motion in multiple directions but isn't involved in the forearm's rotational movement.

Option C - Ellipsoid joint: An ellipsoid joint is a type of joint found in the wrist. It allows for movement in two planes but not rotation around a single axis. Option D - Ball and socket joint: A ball and socket joint is found in the hip and shoulder joints and does not play a significant role in the rotational movement of the forearm.

questions.question: Identify the anatomical structure marked in the given image.

explanation.text: The pointed structure in the shown image is the medial boundary of the anatomical snuffbox which is away from the thumb formed by the extensor pollicis longus muscle. Incorrect Options: Option A - Abductor pollicis brevis: The abductor pollicis brevis muscle in the forearm assists in thumb abduction and borders the anatomical snuffbox.

Option B - Extensor pollicis brevis: The extensor pollicis brevis muscle, situated in the forearm, extends the thumb and lies alongside the anatomical snuffbox. Option C - Abductor pollicis longus: The abductor pollicis longus muscle, in the forearm, aids in wrist abduction and lies near the proximal border of the anatomical snuffbox.

questions.question: Which of the following bones forms the posterior pillar of the medial longitudinal arch?

explanation.text: Each longitudinal arch has: (a) two pillars, (b) a summit, and (c) joints. Medial Longitudinal Arch The medial longitudinal arch is made up of the calcaneum, talus, navicular, three cuneiform bones, and the medial three metatarsals. a) Pillars: The medial half of the calcaneum forms the posterior pillar of the medial longitudinal arch.

The heads of the medial three metatarsals form the anterior pillar of the arch. b) Summit: The talus is located at the highest point (summit) of this arch and acts as its keystone. c) Joints: The main joints involved in the medial longitudinal arch are the talocalcaneonavicular joint and the subtalar joint. Lateral Longitudinal Arch The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneum, cuboid, and lateral two metatarsals.

It is low and nearly touches the ground, helping to support body weight during walking and running. a) Pillars: The posterior pillar is formed by the lateral tubercle of the calcaneum. The anterior pillar is formed by the heads of the lateral two metatarsals. b) Summit: The summit is at the level of the articular facets on the superior surface of the calcaneum, near the subtalar joint. c) Joints: The main joint is the calcaneocuboid joint.
The arch is lower and less flexible than the medial arch, designed to transmit weight and thrust. Reference:

questions.question: Identify X.

explanation.text: The linea semilunaris is a curved groove that runs from the tip of the 9th costal cartilage to the pubic tubercle. It is located a few centimeters lateral to the midline and corresponds to the outer border of the rectus abdominis muscle.
**Linea alba (Option B):** The linea alba is a tendinous raphe that separates the two rectus muscles. This midline groove divides the anterior abdominal wall into two halves, right and left.

**Spino-umbilical Line (Option C):** Also known as the McBurney’s line, is an imaginary line that extends from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS). The point at the junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd of this line corresponds to the McBurney’s point. The base of the appendix lies deep to this point, and it is commonly used in diagnosing acute appendicitis, as tenderness in this area is a key clinical sign.

**Addison’s plane (Option D):** Also known as the Transpyloric Plane, is an imaginary horizontal plane that passes through the midpoint of the line connecting the suprasternal notch to the pubic symphysis.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male presents with a foot drop and weakness in the dorsiflexion of the great toe. He mentions a recent history of a herniated lumbar disc. There is decreased sensation over the dorsum of the foot and the first web space between the great toe and the second toe. Which dermatome and root value are most likely involved?

explanation.text: Foot Drop indicates weakness in dorsiflexion, primarily controlled by the L5 nerve root through the deep peroneal nerve. The L5 dermatome supplies sensation to the dorsum of the foot and the 1st web space between the great toe and the 2nd toe. The patient's decreased sensation in these areas indicates L5 nerve root involvement.

A herniated lumbar disc (most common type—paradiscal), particularly between L4-L5 > L5-S1, can compress the L5 nerve root, leading to the symptoms described. Dermatomes of the lower limb The area of skin supplied by a spinal nerve is termed a dermatome Lower Limb Innervation: Originates from the ventrolateral body wall opposite spinal segments L1–S3. Primarily innervated by the ventral rami of these segments.

Except the superomedial gluteal region is innervated by the dorsal rami of L1–L3 and S1–S3. Limb Bud Orientation: Initially it has preaxial (great toe) and postaxial (little toe) borders. The limb bud rotates medially by 90°, repositioning the great toe medially and the little toe laterally. After rotation, dermatomes are arranged: Preaxial border: L1–L4 (above downward). Postaxial border: S1–S3 (below upward).
Region Dermatome Nerve Supply Heel (Skin on the heel) S1 The posterior tibial nerve has two branches Lateral plantar nerve S1 towards the little toe. Medial plantar nerve L5 towards the great toe.

The popliteal region, posterior thigh (middle), calf, perineal region S2 Posterior cutaneous nerve Lateral foot, dorsum of the foot (Little toe) S1 (Option B) Sural nerve First web space (Dorsum) L5 (Option A) Deep peroneal nerve Medial aspect of leg (Medial malleolus) L4 (Option C) Saphenous nerve Inguinal region (Proximal lower limb) L1 (Option D) Ilioinguinal nerve, Genitofemoral nerve Anterior thigh L2, L3, L4 (Lateral to medial) Femoral nerve Medial thigh L2, L3, L4 Obturator nerve Perineum S2, S3, S4 Pudendal nerve

questions.question: Identify the muscle/muscle head that is not included in the hamstring group of muscles.

options.A: Image a (Long head of biceps femoris)
options.B: Image b (Short head of biceps femoris)

explanation.text: The part marked as “b” in the image is the short head of the biceps femoris, which is not a part of the hamstring group of muscles. (a) Long head of biceps femoris (b) Short head of biceps femoris (c) Semitendinosus (d) Semimembranosus Hamstrings include semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris (long head) and ischial head (Hamstring portion) of adductor magnus They are biarticular muscles that cross both the hip and knee joints, integrating hip extension with knee flexion.

It is important for movement, and stability, and is commonly tested for injury. The characteristic features of hamstring muscles are: All arise from the ischial tuberosity. All are inserted into one of the bones of the leg. All are supplied by tibial part of the sciatic nerve. All are flexors of the knee and extensors of the hip joint.

**Semitendinosus (Option C):** Semimembranosus (Option D) Biceps Femoris Attachments Ischial tuberosity via common tendon with biceps femoris Inserts on the medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus) Ischial tuberosity (long, flat tendon) Inserts on medial tibial condyle and forms oblique popliteal

questions.question: Which of the following muscles is/are supplied by the Nerve to the obturator internus?

explanation.text: The nerve to obturator internus innervates both the obturator internus and superior gemellus muscles. It arises from the anterior divisions of the sacral plexus, originating from the L5, S1, and S2 nerve roots.

Quadratus femoris and Gamellus inferior are supplied by Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4, 5, S1) Obturator Internus: Attachments Origin: Pelvic surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding bones Insertion: On the medial surface of the greater trochanter Vascular Supply Main supply: gemellar branches of the internal pudendal artery Intrapelvic and extrapelvic parts: branches of the obturator artery Innervation Nerve to obturator internus (L5, S1, S2) Actions Laterally rotates the extended thigh.

Abducts the flexed thigh. Gemellus Superior and Gamellus Inferior: Gemellus Superior (smaller than G. inferior) Gamellus Inferior Attachments Origin: Arises from the dorsal surface of the ischial spine Blends with the upper border of obturator internus tendon Insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter.
Origin: Arises from the upper part of the ischial tuberosity Blends with the lower border of obturator internus tendon Insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter.

Vascular Supply Supplied by internal pudendal artery, inferior gluteal artery, and sometimes superior gluteal artery Mainly by the medial circumflex femoral artery Innervation Nerve to obturator internus (L5, S1, S2) Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4, L5, S1) Actions Assists obturator internus in lateral rotation of the thigh May assist in abduction of the flexed thigh Rotates the extended thigh laterally May contribute to abduction of the flexed thigh Quadratus Femoris: Attachments Origin: Arises from the ischial tuberosity Insertion: Trochanteric crest of the femur Vascular Supply Inferior gluteal artery and medial circumflex femoral artery Innervation Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4, L5, S1) Actions Produces lateral rotation of the thigh

questions.question: Which among the following structures do not pass through both the greater and lesser sciatic foramen?

explanation.text: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh only passes through the greater sciatic foramen and not the lesser foramen. Structures passing through greater and lesser sciatic foramen: Greater sciatic notch/foramen/gateway of gluteal region Lesser sciatic notch The piriformis, emerging from the pelvis, fills the foramen almost completely. It is the key muscle of the region.

Structures passing above the piriformis are: Superior gluteal nerve Superior gluteal vessels Structures passing below the piriformis are: Inferior gluteal nerve Inferior gluteal vessels Sciatic nerve The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh Nerve to quadratus femoris Nerve to obturator internus (Option C) Internal pudendal vessels (Option B) Pudendal nerve (Option A) Tendon of obturator internus Pudendal nerve (Option A) Internal pudendal vessels (Option B) Nerve to obturator internus (Option C) The upper and lower parts of the foramen are filled up by the origins of the two gemelli muscles.
